The practical question is not only whether such proof systems are mathematically sound. Developers also need to know whether a proof can be produced quickly, checked quickly, sent over a network cheaply, and trusted under the security assumptions of the application. This paper serves that choice point. It compares two major families, zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs, not as abstract names but as deployable systems with different costs. The paper asks which proof system fits which real situation when speed, proof size, trusted setup, transparency, and post-quantum security pull in different directions.
563.wh: The hard part is that zero-knowledge proof systems are judged by several demands that do not naturally improve together. A system can make very small proofs but require a trusted setup, meaning some initial secret material must be produced and destroyed correctly. Another system can avoid that setup, making the process more transparent, but pay with larger proofs or slower proof creation. The abstract says the theoretical foundations are already well studied, but real-world performance remains less understood. That gap matters because a protocol designer cannot deploy a theorem; they deploy code on hardware with limited CPU, memory, and network capacity. Proof generation time, verification latency, proof size, and CPU bottlenecks are different kinds of cost. The best choice depends on who creates proofs, who verifies them, how often each action happens, whether a trusted ceremony is acceptable, and whether future quantum attacks matter.
563.naive: A smart beginner might read the theory and pick the system with the best asymptotic story, or choose one familiar construction and assume its published security claims settle the decision. Another beginner move is to compare only one visible metric, such as proof size, and declare the smaller proof better. Both shortcuts fail because the deployment problem has several constraints at once. A tiny proof is less attractive if verification is slower or if the application cannot tolerate trusted setup. A transparent proof is less attractive if generating it takes too long or if the proof is too large for the communication path. The paper exists because the simple winner depends on actual implementation behavior, not on a single headline property.
563.ap: The core move is to put two dominant proof styles through the same practical lens. The paper chooses zk-SNARKs represented by Groth16 and zk-STARKs, uses publicly available reference implementations, and runs them on a consumer-grade ARM platform. That keeps the comparison close to the kind of machine a developer might actually have, rather than an idealized setting. It then measures the concrete events a protocol cares about: how long proof generation takes, how long verification takes, how large the proof becomes, and where CPU time is spent. The result is a map of tradeoffs. In the reported results, zk-SNARKs generate proofs 68 times faster and make proofs 123 times smaller, but they verify slower and require trusted setup. zk-STARKs generate larger proofs more slowly, but verify faster, remain transparent, and are described as post-quantum secure.
563.mech: The mechanism starts with the same basic job for both systems: there is a statement to be checked and private evidence behind it. The prover must transform that private evidence into a proof object that convinces a verifier without exposing the evidence itself. For Groth16, the zk-SNARK path uses its reference implementation to create a compact proof under setup material prepared before ordinary proving begins. The experiment records how long that creation takes, how large the resulting proof is, and how much work the verifier needs to accept or reject it. For the zk-STARK path, the reference implementation performs the parallel job without relying on trusted setup. It produces a proof using a different execution model, then the experiment measures the same outward quantities: generation time, verification latency, proof size, and CPU profile. The comparison is therefore not just a yes-or-no security comparison. It is a pipeline comparison. Inputs are proof tasks and implementations; transformations are the prover and verifier computations; measured outputs are elapsed time, proof bytes, and CPU hotspots. The CPU profiling matters because it points below the top-line numbers. If one system spends most effort in a different part of computation than the other, then future engineering work should target different bottlenecks.
563.math: The main mathematical idea is verification without disclosure. In everyday terms, the prover wants to show that a hidden path reaches a public destination without showing the path. The verifier should learn that the claim checks out, but should not learn the secret witness. That requires turning a computation into a checkable object. A proof system compresses the work into evidence that the verifier can test. The tradeoff is compression versus trust and cost: a very compact proof can save communication, but the way it is constructed may require setup assumptions or expensive preparation. SNARKs and STARKs are both ways of making computation checkable, but they make different architectural bargains. The paper also uses measurement as a mathematical comparison tool: each system is mapped into numbers for generation time, verification time, proof size, and CPU use. Those numbers are not merely scores; they describe scarce resources. Time measures processor effort, size measures communication and storage, and verification latency measures how quickly a relying party can check claims. The useful principle is constrained choice under multiple costs. No single number captures the whole system, so the paper compares several quantities side by side and asks which constraint dominates in a given application.
563.dots: This paper sits in the privacy and security part of the conference because it asks what information can safely cross a boundary. It is a close relative of work on constrained sharing, where systems try to pass useful evidence while blocking private details. Federated learning papers face a similar shape: local holders want to contribute patterns without exposing records. Security measurement papers also share the paper's attitude that a formal promise must be tested against deployed behavior. The nearest concept is information: a proof must carry enough information to convince the verifier, but not enough to reconstruct the secret. It also connects to systems tradeoffs. Like efficiency papers that budget time, memory, or communication, this work treats cryptographic design as something that must fit hardware. The theme is zero-knowledge proof systems, but the broader question is common across privacy, blockchains, secure computation, and protocol design: how can a system prove compliance when disclosure itself is the danger?
563.ww: The comparison works because it refuses to treat proof systems as only formal objects. Formal theory can say that a construction is secure or has favorable abstract costs, but developers feel the costs through code paths, processor cycles, verification delays, and network payloads. By running public implementations on the same consumer ARM platform, the paper controls the comparison enough that the measured differences point to the systems rather than to unrelated hardware choices. The findings make intuitive sense as a resource exchange. Groth16 zk-SNARKs buy fast proof generation and very small proofs by accepting trusted setup and slower verification in the measured setting. zk-STARKs buy transparency and post-quantum security while paying more at proof creation and proof size. CPU profiling strengthens the explanation because it shows that these outcomes come from different computational bottlenecks, not only from surface implementation accidents. That gives protocol designers a more usable reason to choose: match the proof system's expensive step to the part of the application that can best afford it.
563.po: The payoff is practical selection guidance. The paper reports that zk-SNARKs generate proofs 68 times faster and make proofs 123 times smaller, while zk-STARKs verify faster and avoid trusted setup. That gives developers and protocol designers a concrete way to reason about applications such as secure computation and privacy-preserving protocols. If proof creation and bandwidth are the main limits, the reported SNARK profile is attractive. If transparent setup, faster checking, and post-quantum security matter more, the reported STARK profile is attractive. The CPU profiles also point researchers toward the parts of each implementation where future speedups would matter most.
563.limits: The abstract supports a careful comparison, but it does not prove every deployment choice. The experiments use publicly available reference implementations and a consumer-grade ARM platform, so results may differ with other libraries, compilers, hardware, circuits, workloads, or implementation maturity. The abstract names Groth16 for zk-SNARKs, so the SNARK conclusions should not automatically cover every SNARK construction. It also reports proof time, verification time, proof size, and CPU profiling, but not full application-level costs such as network congestion, integration complexity, developer error, or setup governance. The trusted setup and post-quantum claims matter only if those assumptions match the threat model of the application being built.

564.bp: Mental-health care is a scarce human service. More people need help than clinics can easily serve, and experts spend time answering clinical questions, triaging concerns, explaining next steps, and keeping language safe and humane. This paper serves that pressure point: it is not trying to replace the therapist described in the abstract, but to build a digital assistant that can support mental-health experts with responses that sound clinically grounded, empathetic, and consistent with therapeutic behavior. The real object being modeled is a professional reply in a sensitive conversation. Such a reply must do several things at once: understand the user's concern, avoid unsafe advice, draw on clinical knowledge, and keep a tone that does not harm trust. coTherapist asks whether a smaller language model can be shaped for this narrow professional role through therapy-specific training, retrieved clinical grounding, and stepwise case reasoning, then checked by rubrics, personality profiling, human experts, and deployment with clinicians.
564.wh: The hard part is that therapeutic support is not just question answering. A general chatbot can produce fluent sentences, but fluency is weak evidence in a clinical setting. A response may be polite while still missing a warning sign, giving advice beyond its competence, ignoring therapeutic boundaries, or sounding empathetic in a way that is not clinically useful. The paper's setting also has a cost pressure: if mental-health access is strained, the system must be practical to run, which is why the abstract stresses a small language model rather than only a very large one. But making the model small creates another tension: it may have less broad knowledge and weaker judgment unless the task is carefully narrowed. The system therefore has to balance several demands that pull against each other: scale versus safety, empathy versus accuracy, learned therapist-like behavior versus grounded clinical evidence, and automatic generation versus human expert trust.
564.naive: A smart beginner might take a general-purpose language model, prompt it to act like a therapist, and ask clinicians to reject bad answers afterward. That can look promising in simple demonstrations because the model already knows many counseling phrases. It fails because therapeutic competence is not a costume. The model may copy surface warmth without knowing when to be cautious, when to ground an answer in clinical knowledge, or how to stay within a support role. Another naive route is a fixed script or checklist. That is safer in narrow cases, but real clinical queries vary in wording, severity, and context, so the script either becomes too rigid or too incomplete. The paper's design moves beyond both shortcuts by combining learned domain behavior, outside clinical retrieval, and explicit reasoning over the case.
564.ap: The core idea is to make a small model behave less like a general talker and more like a trained assistant with a defined clinical role. The paper does this with three linked moves. First, domain-specific fine-tuning shows the model examples of the kind of therapeutic responses it should imitate, so it learns patterns of wording, caution, and professional stance from the target setting. Second, retrieval augmentation gives the model a way to bring relevant clinical material into the answer instead of relying only on what is stored inside its learned parameters. Third, agentic reasoning, meaning an organized process for thinking through the query before answering, helps the system treat a clinical question as a case that needs judgment rather than a prompt that needs decorative empathy. The paper then evaluates not only relevance, but empathy, therapist-consistent personality traits, trustworthiness, safety, and use by clinical experts.
564.mech: The mechanism begins with a clinical query, the sort of question or situation where a mental-health expert might need support. The small language model is not left in its general state. It has first been adjusted on domain material so that, when it sees a mental-health query, its ordinary next-answer habits are closer to therapeutic competencies than to casual web conversation. When a new query arrives, the system also uses retrieval: it searches for relevant clinical grounding and brings that material into view for the response process. This matters because the answer should be tied to clinical knowledge rather than only to remembered language patterns. The agentic reasoning part then organizes the answer-making process. In plain terms, the system considers the case, uses the retrieved evidence, and forms a response that should match the role of a careful therapeutic assistant. The output is a generated reply. The paper checks that output in several ways: comparison on clinical queries against contemporary baselines for relevance and groundedness, a T-BARS rubric for therapeutic behavior, psychometric profiling for empathy and therapist-consistent personality traits, human evaluation by domain experts for accuracy, trustworthiness, and safety, and deployment testing by clinical experts. The mechanism is therefore both a generation pipeline and a checking pipeline.
564.math: The main mathematical idea is learning from examples: turn many cases of desired behavior into adjustable habits inside a model. Fine-tuning means the model is shown domain-specific input-output patterns and its internal settings are changed so that therapist-like responses become more likely for similar future queries. This is a form of error reduction: define, through examples and evaluation, what a better answer looks like, then shift the model toward that behavior. Retrieval adds a second idea, similarity search. A new clinical query is compared with stored clinical material, and the closest useful evidence is brought forward. Closeness here is not moral truth; it is a measured resemblance between the current need and available material, so bad retrieval can still mislead. Agentic reasoning adds structured choice over steps: the system decides how to use the query and retrieved evidence before producing an answer. The evaluations use scoring and human judgment. T-BARS turns therapeutic behavior into categories that can be rated, while psychometric profiling treats empathy and personality consistency as measurable response patterns. The tradeoff is adaptation versus reliability: the model must specialize enough to be useful in mental health, but every learned and retrieved signal must be checked because clinical safety cannot be inferred from fluency alone.
564.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas. It belongs with language-model work because it asks how a fluent model can be made dependable in a real task rather than merely articulate. It also belongs with retrieval-augmented systems: outside evidence is treated as a grounding source, much like other papers that fetch documents or graph facts before generating an answer. Its agentic reasoning connects it to tool-use and agent papers, where the important problem is not just saying something, but following a controlled sequence of steps. The repo's learning concept file explicitly groups coTherapist with papers where useful behavior is easier to demonstrate than to hand-code; here the demonstrated behavior is clinical style, caution, and empathy. It also sits near trust and explainability work because the abstract does not stop at automatic scores. It uses T-BARS, psychometric profiling, domain-expert review, and deployment testing to ask whether the behavior deserves clinical confidence.
564.ww: The method should work better than the naive approach because each component repairs a different weakness. Domain-specific fine-tuning narrows the model's habits. Instead of asking a general model to improvise therapeutic behavior from a role instruction, it repeatedly exposes the system to the kind of response the authors want, making professional tone and clinical caution part of the model's usual behavior in this setting. Retrieval repairs the knowledge problem. If the answer needs clinical grounding, the system can consult relevant material rather than depend only on what the small model retained during training. Agentic reasoning repairs the single-shot response problem by making the model treat the query as something to reason through. The evaluation design also strengthens the claim. Relevance alone would not be enough, so the paper checks empathy, therapist-consistent traits, accuracy, trustworthiness, safety, and clinical-expert deployment. These checks fit the real goal: a mental-health support system must be judged as behavior in context, not as isolated text.
564.po: The payoff is a path toward digital mental-health tools that are cheaper and easier to scale than systems built only around very large models, while still being shaped for a clinical support role. According to the abstract, coTherapist generates responses that are more relevant and clinically grounded than contemporary baselines on clinical queries. It also shows high empathy and therapist-consistent personality traits under the authors' T-BARS rubric and psychometric profiling. Human domain experts judged the responses accurate, trustworthy, and safe, and clinical experts deployed and tested the system. Grounded in the abstract, the practical capability is expert-supporting response generation, not proof of autonomous therapy.
564.limits: The abstract leaves important assumptions open. The system depends on the quality and coverage of the domain-specific fine-tuning data, the retrieved clinical material, and the expert evaluations. If clinical queries differ from the tested cases, or if a user presents risk signals outside the system's learned examples, the behavior may not hold. Similar retrieved evidence can be incomplete or inappropriate for a particular person. Rubrics and psychometric profiles measure response patterns, but they do not prove real therapeutic outcomes. Deployment by clinical experts is valuable, but the abstract does not specify duration, scale, patient population, or failure handling. The safest reading is that coTherapist supports experts under supervision, not that it replaces clinical judgment.

565.bp: Online finance is built on openness. People can create accounts, send money, buy things, and interact with services through the web without showing up at a bank branch. That openness is useful, but it also gives fraudsters room to hide inside ordinary activity. A payment, account, device, merchant, and recipient may each look acceptable when inspected alone, yet together they may form a pattern that harms vulnerable users and weakens trust in digital finance. This paper serves the practical job of finding those harmful cases in web-based financial networks. The paper treats fraud detection as a relationship problem rather than a single-record problem: a transaction is judged not only by its own features, but by how it fits with neighboring accounts and with several views of behavior. Its proposed model, HIMVH, is designed for two fraud realities named in the abstract: rare fraud cases are easy to drown out, and sophisticated fraud can imitate normal behavior.
565.wh: The hard part is that finance data is uneven and adversarial. Uneven means legitimate transactions are common while important fraud cases sit in the long tail: they appear rarely, so a learner can become very good at recognizing normal behavior while giving too little attention to the unusual cases that matter most. Adversarial means fraudsters are not random noise. They try to look harmless. A camouflaged transaction may copy the timing, amount, or local relationship style of ordinary users, so a detector that asks only whether a transaction resembles common behavior can be fooled. Graph neural networks, meaning models that pass evidence between linked accounts, transactions, or entities, help because neighbors provide context. But the abstract says existing graph-based detectors still struggle when rare cases are hidden inside a large normal majority and when malicious behavior is arranged to mimic benign behavior. The detector must therefore notice small conflicts, not just obvious strangeness.
565.naive: A smart beginner would first collect transaction features, connect related accounts or transactions in a graph, and train a graph model to label suspicious cases. The model would let connected records share evidence: if an account is near other risky accounts, raise its risk score. This works when fraud is common enough to teach the model and when fraud looks clearly different from normal use. It fails in the setting described here because the training signal is dominated by legitimate behavior. Rare fraud can be treated as accidental noise. It also fails against camouflage: if a fraudulent transaction copies ordinary patterns in one view, such as amount or timing, a simple graph model may smooth it toward its benign neighbors and make the suspicious signal weaker.
565.ap: The core idea is to look for mismatch rather than only looking for abnormal appearance. HIMVH is described as hippocampus-inspired because the paper borrows two ordinary detection ideas from brain function: noticing conflict between a scene and expectations, and noticing when what arrives does not match what should have arrived. The model first compares multiple transaction views and asks whether they agree. A user may look normal by amount, but strange by recipient pattern; normal by device, but strange by neighborhood behavior. The cross-view inconsistency module tries to capture those small contradictions and behavioral differences. Then the novelty-aware hypergraph module asks a local question: given the surrounding neighborhood, what features would this record be expected to have, and how far does it deviate? A hypergraph, explained plainly, lets one relationship connect more than two things, which fits financial events involving accounts, transactions, devices, merchants, and other grouped evidence.
565.mech: The mechanism begins with web finance records that can be viewed in several ways. The abstract does not list the exact views, so the safe reading is broad: each view is a different description of transaction behavior or relationships, such as feature patterns and neighborhood structure. First, HIMVH represents the financial system as a multi-view hypergraph. Instead of treating every connection as a simple pair, the hypergraph can group several related entities into one higher-order relation, which is useful when fraud depends on a bundle of participants or behaviors rather than one edge. Second, the cross-view inconsistency perception module compares what the different views say about the same transaction or entity. It looks for subtle discrepancies and behavioral heterogeneity: cases where the surface story in one view does not line up with the story in another. Third, the novelty-aware module uses neighborhood expectations. It estimates what a record should look like from nearby records, then measures feature deviations from those expectations. Fourth, those deviations control how messages are reweighted as information moves through the hypergraph. Messages that reveal novelty or mismatch can receive more influence, while ordinary neighbor evidence can be treated with less alarm. The output is a fraud detection score or label that is meant to be more sensitive to camouflaged and rare fraud patterns.
565.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing work here. The first is graph reasoning: represent accounts, transactions, and related finance objects as points connected by relationships, then let evidence travel through those relationships. The risk is that neighbors can mislead when a fraudster deliberately places bad behavior near normal-looking activity. The second idea is higher-order grouping through hypergraphs. A normal graph link says two things are related; a hypergraph relation can say a whole set belongs together. That matters when fraud is not visible in one pair but appears in a coordinated pattern across several entities or views. The third idea is measuring inconsistency. Each view is like a separate witness. The model compares witnesses and looks for disagreement that is small but meaningful. The fourth idea is novelty detection, which means judging surprise relative to an expectation rather than judging rarity in the whole population. Here the expectation comes from the neighborhood: what should this record look like if it followed local behavior? Finally, adaptive reweighting is a scoring-and-budgeting move. When messages pass through the graph, the model changes their strength based on deviation, balancing local evidence against the danger of smoothing away rare fraud.
565.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of graph learning, fraud detection, anomaly detection, and web trust. Its neighbors in the conference are papers that ask how to find rare harmful behavior when normal behavior supplies most of the examples. The shared pressure is not just classification; it is deciding which small irregularities deserve attention before harm spreads. It also connects to broader graph papers because it relies on the idea that relationships carry evidence, while openly confronting the failure case where relationship evidence can be used as camouflage. The multi-view part connects to retrieval, recommendation, and multimodal reasoning in a looser way: many systems now compare several partial descriptions of the same object and search for agreement or conflict among them. The novelty-aware part connects to probability and anomaly work, because it asks what should be expected from repeated local patterns and then flags departures. Its family is fraud and anomaly detection, with a specific focus on financial web harms.
565.ww: The method should improve over the naive graph approach because it changes the question from "does this look common?" to "does this fit all the evidence that surrounds it?" Camouflage is strongest when a fraudster only needs to fool one view of the data. If the detector checks several views, the attacker has a harder job: a behavior that looks normal by amount may still conflict with its transaction neighborhood, feature pattern, or higher-order group. Long-tailed fraud is also better served by local novelty than by global frequency. A rare transaction is not automatically fraudulent, and a common-looking transaction is not automatically safe. What matters is whether the record violates expectations created by its own neighborhood. Reweighting messages based on those deviations helps prevent ordinary majority behavior from washing out rare signals. The hippocampus analogy is useful only as a design guide, not proof: the real reason to expect success is that mismatch and local surprise are exactly where camouflaged fraud leaves evidence when surface similarity is misleading.
565.po: The payoff is a detector aimed at the two cases that financial platforms most need to handle: fraud that is rare enough to be overlooked and fraud that is disguised enough to resemble normal behavior. The abstract reports experiments on six web-based financial fraud datasets and says HIMVH improves average AUC by 6.42%, F1 by 9.74%, and AP by 39.14% over 15 compared models. In practical terms, the claimed benefit is not just a higher score; it is better sensitivity to hidden fraudulent behavior in open web finance systems, where missed cases can directly harm users and reduce trust in digital financial services.
565.limits: The abstract supports the mechanism and reported gains, but it does not prove that the method will generalize to every financial platform or every future fraud strategy. The approach assumes that useful transaction views exist, that camouflaged fraud creates cross-view conflicts, and that neighborhood expectations are informative rather than themselves corrupted. If fraudsters coordinate large normal-looking neighborhoods, local expectations may become less trustworthy. The hypergraph structure also depends on how relationships are built from raw finance data; poor grouping could hide the signal. The neuroscience inspiration should be treated as an analogy for mismatch detection, not evidence that the model works like a human brain.

566.bp: A web recommendation system is trying to follow a person whose interests are moving while the system is watching. Someone may start with travel photos, drift toward hiking gear, pause on restaurant videos, and later return to a destination guide. The platform sees interactions across several kinds of content, not only one list of products or articles. This paper serves that setting: recommending useful items when user interest is a path through time, shaped by text, images, videos, and links among users and items. The abstract argues that many recommenders freeze this path into separate snapshots or draw an over-simple line through it. That misses the fact that interest can move continuously and with direction. Drifting with Intent treats interest as something that changes moment by moment, then tries to generate a personalized trajectory that points toward meaningful content instead of treating future preference as a random next step.
566.wh: The hard part is that user behavior is both connected and time-sensitive. A click today may be a continuation of yesterday's topic, a short detour, or a sign that the user is leaving one interest for another. Multimodal platforms add another difficulty: items are not described by one signal. A video, image, caption, category, and past co-click pattern may each say something different about why the item matters. If the system records only discrete snapshots, it loses the motion between them. If it records only a simple trajectory, it may miss different granularities: one broad travel interest can contain narrower interests in flights, hotels, food, and outdoor gear. The abstract also contrasts directed drift with diffusion-style randomness. The tension is deciding whether the user's next interest should be modeled as wandering noise or as motion pulled by content that has relational and temporal meaning.
566.naive: A smart beginner would build a timeline of user actions, make one profile for each time window, and recommend items similar to the latest profile. That is reasonable because recent behavior often matters most. It fails in three ways. First, fixed windows cut a continuous process into artificial blocks, so the system may miss gradual movement. Second, one profile can average together several simultaneous interests, such as work research and entertainment browsing. Third, simple similarity to the latest actions treats all movement as local copying: show more of what was just clicked. The abstract's point is that interest has direction. A user is not merely near past items; they may be drifting toward a future content region that has not yet been clicked.
566.ap: The core idea is to model user interest as a continuous-time process with intent. Continuous-time means the model does not have to pretend that preference changes only at a few recorded timestamps. A stochastic process is a way to describe movement when the next position is uncertain; here it is governed by stochastic differential equations, which are rules for how a changing quantity moves while allowing noise. The paper's distinctive claim is that the movement is not just random spreading. It is directed drift toward meaningful content. To supply the map on which that drift happens, the method uses a multi-granularity hypergraph encoder. A hypergraph link can connect more than two things, such as a user, several items, and a shared context. Multi-granularity means it can represent broad and narrow interaction patterns. A unified solver then generates personalized interest trajectories across both time and relationships.
566.mech: The mechanism begins with user-item interaction records from multimodal web platforms. Each record is evidence that a user touched some content at some time, while the content itself may carry multiple media signals. First, the multi-granularity hypergraph encoder organizes these records into relational groups. At a small grain, it can capture specific user-item contacts. At a larger grain, it can capture cross-scale patterns, such as groups of users, items, and content types that repeatedly appear together. The encoder turns those groups into a structured state for the user: not a single flat profile, but a description of where the user's interests sit in a relational content map. Next, the model treats interest evolution as a continuous path through that map. The stochastic differential equation supplies the update rule: from the current state, one part describes intentional drift toward promising content regions, while another part leaves room for uncertainty because user behavior is never perfectly predictable. A unified SDE solver follows this rule across temporal and relational dimensions to generate a personalized trajectory. During training, the generative side learns to produce plausible interest paths, and the discriminative side learns to separate better recommendations from worse ones. The abstract says these are co-optimized in one parameter space, so generation and ranking precision are balanced without redundant twin networks. The output is both a ranked recommendation signal and an interpretable path showing how interests moved.
566.math: The main mathematical idea is a continuous-time stochastic process. In everyday terms, the model treats interest like a moving point whose exact future location is uncertain, but whose movement is not arbitrary. A stochastic differential equation is a rule for motion under uncertainty: it says how the current state changes over an infinitesimal slice of time, combining a directed push with random variation. The directed push is drift. In this paper, drift means the model believes user interest is being pulled toward meaningful content, not merely scattering in every direction. The second mathematical object is a hypergraph. A normal graph link joins two things; a hypergraph link can join a whole group. That fits recommendation because an interaction often involves a user, an item, a modality, a time, and a larger behavioral context together. Multi-granularity modeling is the idea that useful evidence exists at several scales, from exact contacts to broader clusters of related behavior. The third idea is co-optimization: deciding what counts as wrong for both trajectory generation and recommendation discrimination, then adjusting shared model settings so both errors shrink. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus discipline. A rich continuous path can describe subtle change, but it must remain tied to observed interactions and ranking goals.
566.dots: This paper belongs to the recommendation family because it addresses the repeated conference problem of choosing a small useful set of items from a huge changing catalog. It is specifically close to multimodal recommendation work such as the repo's MSCA record, which also worries that behavior and media content must be made compatible before ranking. The difference is that Drifting with Intent emphasizes movement through time, not only alignment among views. It also connects to graph-augmented recommendation records because the hypergraph treats relationships as carriers of evidence: neighbors and groups help explain where interest may move. It sits near sequential recommendation papers because the order of actions matters, but it pushes beyond a plain sequence by using continuous motion rather than isolated steps. Finally, it connects to generative recommendation because it does not only score existing candidates; it generates an interest trajectory that can be inspected as an explanation of why certain content becomes relevant.
566.ww: The method should improve over the naive snapshot approach because it preserves the thing snapshots destroy: motion. If a user's behavior gradually changes, a model with continuous time can represent the path between observations instead of treating each logged action as a disconnected update. The drift term helps because recommendation is usually not pure wandering. People follow purposes, moods, projects, and curiosity trails; the next useful item is often in the direction implied by several previous interactions, not just near the last clicked item. The hypergraph helps because interests are relational. A content item can be meaningful because of its image, text, co-viewed neighbors, and the user group that tends to choose it. Group links let evidence travel across those connected pieces without reducing every relationship to pairwise contacts. Co-optimizing generation and discrimination also matters. A generated path that looks plausible but does not rank good items is not useful, while a ranker with no path may be opaque and short-sighted. Training both goals together should make the trajectory both predictive and recommendation-relevant.
566.po: The payoff is a recommender that can treat user preference as a living trajectory rather than a stale profile. The abstract claims experiments across eight diverse datasets show better recommendation quality than state-of-the-art methods and produce interpretable interest trajectories. Grounded practically, that means a platform could recommend not only by asking what the user liked before, but by estimating where the user's interest is moving across content types and relationships. The interpretability claim is important: the system is meant to reveal how interests evolve, giving practitioners more than a ranked list with no account of the motion behind it.
566.limits: The abstract is truncated at the end, so some experimental and interpretation details are not visible in the provided input. The method assumes user interests really can be represented as continuous directed trajectories; if behavior is mostly erratic, coerced by interface exposure, or driven by one-time events, drift may give false structure. It also assumes the hypergraph captures meaningful cross-scale relations rather than popularity shortcuts. Multimodal signals must be relevant to user choice, and timestamps must be informative enough to support continuous-time modeling. The abstract reports eight-dataset gains, but it does not prove long-term user satisfaction, fairness, privacy behavior, serving cost, or stability when catalogs and user goals change rapidly.

567.bp: The ordinary problem is a web post that asks people to believe a story using both words and pictures. The words may make a claim, while the image supplies emotional force or apparent proof. A fake post can therefore lie in several ways: the text can be false, the image can be altered, or the image can be real but placed beside words that change its meaning. This paper serves systems that must decide whether such multimodal information is trustworthy before it spreads through feeds, search, and social sharing. The paper argues that a detector cannot treat the picture as a decorative add-on to the text. It must inspect local visual clues, such as small forged regions, global visual clues, such as a whole-image anomaly, and the semantic relation between text and image. SVPF-Net is proposed as a way to combine these clues with knowledge-guided priorities instead of simply mixing all signals at the end.
567.wh: The hard part is that fake multimodal information often looks ordinary when each part is checked alone. A cropped or edited image may have only a small forged area, so a whole-image scan can miss it. A post can also have an image that is visually plausible but globally strange for the claim being made. Text adds another difficulty: the words may carry high-quality semantic information about entities, events, or claims, but traditional multimodal methods may let the text and image interact only weakly. If the two streams are processed separately and fused late, the model may never ask the important question: which visual evidence supports, contradicts, or changes the meaning of the words? The abstract also points to global structural anomalies, meaning the problem is not only pixel tampering. The detector must judge whether local visual details, whole-image patterns, and textual meaning fit together as one credible story.
567.naive: A smart beginner would build two detectors: one reads the text, one checks the image, and a final rule averages their scores. That feels reasonable because fake news has words and pictures, so each side can vote. It fails because the lie may live in the relationship, not in either side alone. The text might be harmless by itself, and the image might be real by itself, while the pairing is misleading. Another beginner move is to scan the image at one scale. That misses the paper's split between local forgeries and global anomalies. Small edits need close inspection, while larger inconsistencies need a broader view. A flat average also assumes text and image deserve equal trust in every case, which the paper explicitly tries to avoid.
567.ap: The core move is to make the visual side more structured before combining it with text, then let the system decide which kind of evidence should matter more during fusion. SVPF-Net first extracts two kinds of image evidence: local clues tied to small forged regions and global clues tied to broader anomaly patterns. It then uses weighted fusion, meaning it builds a combined visual description by assigning different strengths to different clues rather than treating all clues as equal. Cross-attention, a scoring mechanism where one part asks which other parts are relevant to it, aligns local and global image features in both directions. After that, the model brings in high-quality textual semantic features and combines them with the enhanced visual representation through modality-priority progressive fusion. In plain terms, the system does not dump text and image into one bucket. It lets each source influence the other while learning which source should lead at each stage.
567.mech: The input is a multimodal news item: text plus visual content. The visual branch first performs dual feature extraction. One extractor is meant to catch local forgery cues, such as a region whose details do not fit the rest of the image. The other is meant to capture global anomaly patterns, such as whole-image structure that looks inconsistent with the surrounding claim. Those two visual descriptions are then passed to a dual-fusion enhancement module. A weighted fusion strategy combines them into a structured visual representation, where the system can preserve both close-up evidence and broad context instead of flattening them into one undifferentiated signal. Next, cross-attention aligns the two visual levels. Cross-attention means that local features are scored against global features, and global features are scored against local features, so each side can select the parts of the other side that explain or challenge it. The resulting visual representation is then fused with textual semantic features. The abstract says this happens through modality-priority progressive fusion, again relying on cross-attention. That implies a staged combination: text and image interact, but the model can give higher priority to the modality that carries more useful evidence for the current example. The output is a detection decision supported by more interpretable semantic evidence about how local image cues, global image anomalies, and text-image meaning fit or conflict.
567.math: The main mathematical idea is learned comparison under unequal evidence. Weighted fusion is a controlled averaging operation: several signals are available, and the system must choose how much each one contributes to the final description. The tradeoff is detail versus stability. Local visual clues may catch a tiny forgery but can be noisy; global clues are steadier but can miss small manipulation. Cross-attention is a relevance table. For each local visual piece, the model assigns scores to global pieces, and for each global piece, it assigns scores back to local pieces. After the scores are turned into weights, the model forms a new description that emphasizes the most related evidence. This fits the paper because forgery is relational: a suspicious patch matters differently depending on the whole image, and a whole-image anomaly becomes clearer when the suspicious local areas are known. The multimodal fusion stage repeats the same principle across text and image. The model is not proving truth logically. It is learning, from labeled examples, which patterns of agreement and disagreement tend to mark fake information. The underlying mathematics is therefore scoring, weighting, comparing, and reducing classification error, where reducing error means adjusting model settings so fake and real examples are separated more reliably.
567.dots: This paper sits where misinformation detection, multimodal vision-language modeling, and anomaly detection meet. Like fraud and anomaly papers, it looks for evidence that appears normal locally but suspicious when context is added. Like retrieval and recommendation papers, it faces a fusion problem: many signals are available, but not every signal deserves the same weight for every case. Like language-model and knowledge-enhanced papers, it treats semantics as more than surface words; the text carries meaning about what the image is supposed to show. The neighboring idea is not simply better image classification. It is cross-source consistency: does one form of evidence support, refine, or contradict another? The fraud-anomaly family record in the repo groups this paper with methods that find hidden inconsistency, and this paper's version of inconsistency is visual-semantic rather than only behavioral or graph-based. Its broader theme is trust on the Web, where detection systems must reason across media because bad actors can move the lie to whichever channel is least inspected.
567.ww: The mechanism should help because it matches the shape of the deception. If a fake item is produced by altering a small image region, then a detector that keeps local visual evidence has a chance to notice the edit. If the deception is more about an image being globally unsuitable for the claim, then a detector that keeps whole-image anomaly information has a chance to notice that broader mismatch. The two kinds of visual evidence also strengthen each other: a local oddity is more meaningful when the rest of the image makes it suspicious, and a global oddity is easier to interpret when local regions explain where the mismatch starts. The text-image fusion helps for the same reason. A post's meaning is built jointly: the words tell the reader what to see, and the image makes the words feel concrete. Modality-priority fusion avoids assuming the same balance in every case. Some examples may be text-led, others image-led, and the model can learn that difference from data.
567.po: The payoff is a detector that is designed for practical multimodal fake news rather than text-only rumor detection or image-only forgery detection. The abstract claims comprehensive experiments validate SVPF-Net's optimal performance and its ability to enhance interpretable semantics. Grounded in the local records, the capability gained is stronger cross-modal semantic interaction: the system can use local image forgeries, global visual anomalies, and textual semantic features together. That gives downstream web platforms a more reliable basis for flagging or ranking suspicious multimodal information, especially when the suspicious signal is distributed across several media channels.
567.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The training data must contain enough examples where local forgeries, global anomalies, and text-image mismatches are labeled in ways the model can learn from. The textual semantic features must be high quality; if the text analysis misunderstands entities or claims, the fusion stage can prioritize the wrong evidence. The abstract does not specify datasets, failure cases, or whether the method handles real images used in misleading contexts without pixel edits. It also does not prove that weighted fusion is interpretable to human fact-checkers, only that semantics are enhanced. Since the method learns from observed patterns, it may fail when new misinformation styles break the learned relationship between visual cues and textual meaning.

568.bp: A large recommender system cannot carefully judge every possible article, video, or product for every user. It usually works like a narrowing funnel: first retrieve a rough pile of possible candidates, then pre-rank that pile, then let more expensive ranking stages examine a smaller set. This paper focuses on the pre-ranking stage, the middle filter that must be fast enough for industrial traffic but accurate enough not to throw away the few items a user might actually value. The real-world object is not a clean list of equally informative examples. It is a mixed stream of candidates coming from rough retrieval, detailed ranking signals, and exposure feedback from what users were shown before. The paper argues that treating all those training cases as if they were the same kind of evidence weakens the pre-ranker. Its answer is to notice candidate difficulty and spend modeling effort where the decision is genuinely hard.
568.wh: The hard part is that pre-ranking sits between two unequal worlds. Retrieval is coarse: it gathers many plausible candidates quickly, including many easy cases that a simple scorer can reject. Later ranking is fine-grained: it compares candidates more carefully and produces richer signals. Exposure feedback adds another complication because it reflects what the system chose to show, not every item the user could have seen. When training examples from these sources are mixed together, they pull the learner in different directions. The abstract calls this gradient conflict: during training, each batch gives a direction for how to change the model, and hard cases can push strongly while easy cases still consume data and computation without teaching much. A single increase in model complexity also wastes effort, because easy candidates do not need a stronger judge while hard candidates may.
568.naive: A smart beginner would build one pre-ranking model, feed it all available training examples, and make the model larger if accuracy is not good enough. That is attractive because it is simple and uses every sample. But the paper says the samples are heterogeneous: they come from rough retrieval, refined ranking behavior, and exposure logs, so they do not all ask the same learning question. Easy samples may already be separable, while hard samples sit near the decision boundary. Mixing them indiscriminately lets their training signals interfere, and uniformly scaling the model spends extra computation on candidates that a lightweight model could already handle.
568.ap: The core idea is to stop pretending that every candidate deserves the same learning path and the same serving cost. Heterogeneity-Aware Adaptive Pre-ranking first separates easy and hard samples, then treats the two groups differently. Easy candidates still pass through lightweight models, so the system keeps broad coverage without paying too much. Hard candidates, where a wrong pre-ranking decision is more likely and more costly, receive stronger modeling. Training is also changed: conflict-sensitive sampling and tailored losses are used so the training signal from one kind of sample does not simply drown out or fight the signal from another. In plain terms, the method turns pre-ranking from one uniform judge into a staged judge that asks, "Is this case obvious, or does it deserve closer inspection?"
568.mech: The mechanism starts with the normal inputs available to an industrial recommender pre-ranker: candidate items produced by retrieval, richer signals from later ranking stages, and feedback from prior exposures. From these, the system forms training instances that differ in difficulty and source. Instead of pooling them into one undifferentiated training set, HAP disentangles easy and hard samples. The abstract does not spell out the exact rule for measuring difficulty, but it does say the separation is used to reduce conflicts among training directions and to allocate computation adaptively. During learning, conflict-sensitive sampling controls which kinds of cases are emphasized, while tailored loss design changes what the model is punished for on each path. A loss is simply a score for how wrong the model was; changing it changes which mistakes the training process cares about most. At serving time, the system applies lightweight models to all candidates, giving cheap coverage across the whole retrieved pile. Then it engages stronger models on the hard candidates, where extra computation is more likely to change the final ordering. The output is a pre-ranked candidate set that should preserve accuracy while avoiding unnecessary cost on obvious cases.
568.math: The main mathematical idea is selective resource allocation under a learned error signal. The system has a scarce resource, computation, and a large pile of candidates. It must decide where extra computation buys information and where it is wasted. Ranking supplies the first object: each candidate receives a score so the system can order many possibilities and pass only promising ones forward. Learning supplies the second object: a loss, meaning a numerical description of what counts as a bad score or bad order. Optimization, in plain language, means repeatedly changing model settings to make that badness smaller. The conflict issue comes from the fact that different examples can suggest different changes. A hard sample may say, "move the boundary this way," while another group of samples pushes elsewhere. HAP responds by separating sample types and giving them dedicated learning paths. Sampling is a mathematical way of deciding which examples are allowed to speak loudly during training. Adaptive computation is a budgeting rule: first spend a small amount everywhere, then spend more only where uncertainty or difficulty justifies it. The tradeoff is accuracy versus cost, with difficulty acting as the guide.
568.dots: This paper belongs to the recommender-system family because it is about choosing a small useful set from a huge candidate pile under uncertainty. It connects directly to ranking: the practical question is which candidates should survive early filtering so later stages can inspect them. It also connects to efficiency and scalability work, because the method treats compute time as a budget that must be spent unevenly rather than expanded everywhere. A neighboring idea is hard-example selection: many learning systems gain more from borderline cases than from examples that are already obvious. Another neighboring idea is multi-stage retrieval, where cheap broad search and expensive careful judgment must cooperate. Compared with fairness or cold-start recommendation papers, this one is less about whose items get exposure and more about whether the pre-ranking training process itself is confused by mixing unlike evidence sources.
568.ww: The approach should work when candidate difficulty is real and measurable enough to guide routing. Easy cases are useful for coverage, but once the system can already separate them, repeatedly spending strong modeling on them gives little new information. Hard cases are different: they are close to the point where the system might keep or discard a candidate, so a small scoring improvement can change what reaches later ranking. Separating easy and hard samples also makes the training signal cleaner. If all samples are mixed, the model tries to satisfy training directions that may be uneven in strength and meaning because the examples come from different sources. Dedicated paths let each subset shape the model in a way suited to its role. The production result in the abstract supports the practical story: Toutiao deployed HAP for nine months and reported improved app usage duration and active days without extra computational cost. That result is consistent with a system that spends effort where ranking mistakes matter most.
568.po: The payoff is a pre-ranking system that aims to be both more accurate and more economical. Instead of making every candidate pass through uniformly stronger machinery, HAP uses lightweight processing for all candidates and stronger processing for hard ones. The abstract reports deployment in Toutiao's production system for nine months, with up to 0.4 percent improvement in user app usage duration and 0.05 percent in active days, without additional computational cost. The paper also releases a large-scale industrial hybrid-sample dataset, which matters because studying source-driven candidate heterogeneity requires realistic mixed training data.
568.limits: The method depends on the system being able to separate easy and hard samples in a way that matches real pre-ranking risk. If the difficulty signal is noisy, biased by exposure history, or different after deployment, computation may be routed to the wrong candidates. The abstract reports gains in Toutiao, but that does not prove the same tradeoff for every platform, item type, or user population. It also does not fully specify in the input evidence how difficulty is measured, how losses are tailored, or how much of the gain comes from sampling versus adaptive model strength.

569.bp: A giant shopping or content platform has a simple-looking problem: new items arrive with almost no history, but the system must decide whether they deserve attention. If the recommender mostly shows items that already have click evidence, the rich get richer. Established items keep receiving exposure, while a new product may never collect enough impressions to prove that some users would like it. AliBoostV2 serves the part of recommendation where the platform deliberately gives cold items extra chances. The paper is not only asking, "Who will click this item right now?" It asks a broader platform question: "Which exposure can help this item become self-sustaining later?" That matters for Alibaba and Taobao because a marketplace needs fresh supply to circulate, sellers need a path out of invisibility, and users need discovery rather than only repeated winners. The abstract frames the system as a production method for balancing immediate click-through rate with longer-term item growth.
569.wh: The hard part is that the platform is choosing under a feedback loop. A click is easy to observe after an item is shown, so click-through rate becomes a tempting target. But exposure itself changes the evidence: items that are shown more often get more chances to be clicked, recommended again, shared, purchased, or noticed by natural traffic. Cold items start with weak evidence not necessarily because they are bad, but because the system has not let enough people see them. A pure click target also treats all clicking users as equal. One user may click and then the item disappears; another may click, buy, share, or otherwise create signals that cause later unpaid traffic. The abstract says AliBoost V1 promoted cold items to users most likely to click them, but still followed the same click-centered goal. That leaves long-term ecosystem health outside the main decision, so short-term accuracy can compete with the growth of new supply.
569.naive: A smart beginner would take every cold item, estimate which users are most likely to click it, and spend the boosting budget on those users. This is sensible because clicks are quick, measurable, and tied to revenue. It fails because it confuses the first response with the whole consequence. If the system only seeks high immediate click probability, it may pick users whose click does not create further natural traffic. It may also miss users who are slightly less likely to click but, when they do, help the item spread. The result is a booster that can raise today's click count while still leaving the item dependent on paid or artificial exposure.
569.ap: AliBoostV2 changes the target from "best clicker" to "best growth-producing exposure that still respects clicks." Its central move is to attach a second value to each possible user-item exposure: the extra natural traffic that would happen because that exposure occurred. The abstract says this is estimated with counterfactual reasoning, meaning the system tries to compare two imagined cases that are alike except for one change: the user was shown the cold item in one case and was not shown it in the other. The difference between those cases is treated as the exposure's growth value. Then a dynamic boosting strategy combines the immediate click signal with this growth signal. It also tracks that users behave differently across time periods, so the best boosting target can change with the moment, not just with the item.
569.mech: The mechanism begins with candidate cold items and candidate users who could receive boosted exposure. For each possible exposure, the system needs at least two kinds of estimates. First, it estimates the ordinary click chance: if this user sees this item now, how likely is the user to click? Second, the Growth Potential Prediction module estimates the extra natural traffic caused by that one exposure. In plain terms, it asks how much later attention would be added beyond what would have happened anyway. To do that, the paper uses counterfactual reasoning: compare an observed or modeled path where the boosting exposure happens against a matched alternative path where it does not happen, then attribute the difference in later natural traffic to the exposure. The dynamic CTR-growth strategy then scores candidate users by both immediate response and growth value. It also captures different interaction patterns across time periods, so a user can be a good growth carrier in one period and less useful in another. The output is a set of selected users who receive boosted delivery for cold items. The production result reported in the abstract is six months of deployment across Alibaba and Taobao main platforms, cold-starting over one billion new items.
569.math: The main mathematical ideas are scoring, ranking, controlled comparison, and multi-goal decision making. Scoring means turning signs about a user, an item, a moment, and past interactions into numbers the system can compare. Ranking means using those numbers to choose which users should receive scarce boosted exposure first. The click score measures immediate response. The growth score measures a different object: expected added natural traffic after an exposure. Counterfactual reasoning is controlled comparison. It asks, "What would have happened to this item if this exposure had not occurred?" Because the platform cannot literally run both histories for the same user and item at the same time, the method must model or estimate the missing alternative. The useful number is the gap between the boosted case and the no-boost case. The final decision is a balancing problem: choose exposures that reduce the mistake of ignoring click-through rate while also reducing the mistake of starving future growth. This math fits because the real resource is limited visibility. Every exposure has an opportunity cost, and the platform needs a principled way to sort users by both near-term and delayed consequences.
569.dots: This paper sits inside the recommender-systems family because it repairs the comparison before making the recommendation. Like pre-ranking work, it must choose a small set from a huge pile under serving pressure, but its special pressure is cold-item growth rather than candidate filtering alone. It also belongs with ranking papers that fight self-reinforcing loops: if previous visibility is rewarded without correction, familiar or popular items keep winning because they were already visible. AliBoostV2 adds a causal flavor to recommendation by asking what an exposure changes, not merely what tends to appear with clicks. That connects it to the conference's broader cause idea: separate a true lever from a surface correlation. It also touches advertising and e-commerce because boosting resembles spending scarce promotion budget. The broader field connection is multi-objective recommendation: the system is no longer sorting only by current user response, but by a negotiated goal involving clicks, gross merchandise value, item discovery, and marketplace health.
569.ww: The approach should work better than the naive click-only booster because it separates two kinds of value that are mixed together in platform logs. Immediate click-through rate tells whether the first shown user is likely to react. Growth potential asks whether that reaction helps the item escape coldness by creating later natural traffic. If two users have the same click chance, the one whose exposure produces more downstream traffic is more valuable for cold-starting. If one user has a slightly higher click chance but little growth value, blindly choosing that user can waste a scarce boost. The counterfactual comparison matters because later traffic may have happened anyway; the system needs to estimate the added traffic caused by the boost, not just count all traffic after it. The dynamic time-aware part also helps because user behavior is not constant. A user who discovers or spreads items in one period may be less useful in another. By updating the CTR-growth tradeoff across time periods, the system can aim boosts where both immediate and delayed signals line up.
569.po: The payoff is a production recommender that treats cold-starting as more than a temporary click lift. The abstract reports deployment across Alibaba and Taobao's main platforms for six months and says the system successfully cold-started over one billion new items. Compared with AliBoost V1, it reports improvements of over 17.54 percent in both clicks and gross merchandise value for cold items within a 180-day period. The practical capability is targeted promotion that can still respect near-term engagement while trying to make new items earn later natural traffic, which is closer to a healthy marketplace than simply buying early impressions.
569.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The system must estimate the missing no-boost alternative well enough that growth value is not just another biased score. Logged platform behavior must contain useful signals about later natural traffic, not only artifacts created by previous recommendation rules. The abstract says there were online analyses and A/B tests, but it does not describe the matching details, the exact features, the budget constraints, or how seller, user, and platform interests were weighted. It also reports Alibaba and Taobao production results, so the claim may depend on their traffic scale, item supply, user behavior, and existing boosting infrastructure. A method that improves cold-item clicks and GMV can still leave questions about diversity, seller fairness, and long-term user satisfaction.
